Medium, Hard, and Grandmaster use minimax with alpha-beta pruning at increasing search depths (1, 2, 3 half-moves). Online mode matches you against real players via ELO-based matchmaking — both sides share the 20-second move timer. A coin toss assigns White or Black at the start of every game.
step6.coinToss: Coin toss assigns White / Black each game
tips: Easy CPU is genuinely random — it will sometimes blunder its Queen on move two.
Grandmaster uses minimax at depth 3 — it plays solid, principled chess at this control.
CPU games do not affect your ELO — only Online matches count toward your rating.

step7.title: Online Play & ELO
step7.description: Online mode connects you to real opponents near your ELO rating. Before the game starts, the interface shows your opponent's ELO and your estimated win chance — a higher percentage means the system expects you to win based on rating difference. After each online game your ELO updates: wins gain points, losses subtract, and draws are roughly neutral. You can forfeit an ongoing online game at any time.
tips: Win chance above 60% means you're the favourite — below 40% means you're the underdog.
Beating a higher-rated opponent earns more ELO than beating an equal one.
Forfeiting counts as a loss and deducts ELO — resign only when the position is truly hopeless.

step0.title: Welcome to Connect Four
step0.description: Drop coloured discs into a 6-row × 7-column blue grid. Gravity pulls each disc to the lowest available row in the chosen column. The first player to align four of their discs — horizontally, vertically, or diagonally — wins. If the board fills with no winner, the game is a draw.
tips: Red always goes first — a coin toss decides whether you play Red or Yellow.
The board has 6 rows and 7 columns; column numbers 1–7 are shown below the board.
Discs fall to the bottom of their column — you can't place one in mid-air.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, hover over a column to preview where your disc will land — a coloured indicator appears above that column. Click any cell in the column to drop your disc. On mobile, tap any cell in the target column. You have 20 seconds per turn; if time runs out, a disc drops in a random open column.
step1.timer: 20 s per turn — random drop on timeout
tips: The ▼ indicator above a column shows exactly which column will receive your disc.
Clicking anywhere within a column — not just at the bottom — drops the disc correctly.
A 20-second timer is shared by both players; your opponent also has 20 s per turn.

step2.title: Dropping Discs
step2.description: Discs always fall to the lowest empty row in a column — you can never float one in mid-air. Once a column has all 6 rows filled, it is closed and can no longer accept discs. The drop animation briefly scales the disc when it lands.
step2.hint: Discs stack from the bottom row upward.
tips: Plan ahead — a full column is permanently blocked for the rest of the game.
Filling columns strategically can force your opponent into unfavourable positions.
The centre column (col 4) is the most valuable: it participates in the most possible four-in-a-row lines.

step3.title: Winning: Four in a Row
step3.description: Connect four discs of your colour in any straight line to win. Lines can run horizontally across a row, vertically up a column, or diagonally in either direction. Winning discs glow with a white border and a bright highlight — Red turns orange and Yellow turns bright yellow.
step3.hint: Four in any direction wins — there are 69 possible winning lines on a 6×7 board.
tips: There are 24 horizontal, 21 vertical, and 24 diagonal winning lines — diagonals are the easiest to miss.
Threats in two different directions simultaneously force your opponent into a no-win situation.
The top row is the last to fill — a threat there is often overlooked.

step4.title: Colours & Draw
step4.description: Red moves first every game. A coin toss decides which colour you play before each game begins. A draw occurs when all 42 cells are filled without either player forming a four-in-a-row. Draws are rare but possible — the board must be completely full.
tips: Because Red goes first, Yellow needs to play more defensively in the early game.
A draw is actually quite rare — most games end in a win for one side.
If you're Yellow, the best opening counter to Red centre is also the centre column.

step5.title: Game Modes & Difficulty
step5.description: CPU mode lets you play against the computer at four levels. Easy plays randomly. Medium, Hard, and Grandmaster use minimax with increasing search depth (2, 4, 6 moves ahead), using heuristics that reward centre control and connected threats. Online matches you against a real player via ELO-based matchmaking with a 20-second timer.
step5.coinToss: Coin toss assigns Red / Yellow each game
tips: Easy CPU plays completely randomly — great for learning threats and patterns.
Grandmaster looks 6 moves ahead with alpha-beta pruning — it prizes centre control heavily.
CPU games don't affect your ELO rating — only Online matches count.

step6.title: Strategy & ELO
step6.description: Control the centre column — a disc in column 4 participates in more four-in-a-row lines than any other position. Always check for opponent threats before placing your own disc. Build double threats: two ways to win at once so your opponent can only block one. Online wins and losses adjust your ELO rating based on the rating difference between you and your opponent.
tips: A 'seven trap' fills column 7 last to force your opponent into giving you a winning row.
Connecting three with an open space on both ends ('open three') is almost impossible to stop.
ELO gains are larger when beating a higher-rated opponent and smaller against a lower-rated one.

step0.title: Welcome to Reversi
step0.description: Reversi (also known as Othello) is played on an 8×8 green board. Each player has an unlimited supply of discs — black and white. The game starts with two black and two white discs placed diagonally in the centre. Black always moves first. Your goal is to have the most discs of your colour on the board when neither player can make another legal move.
tips: Black always moves first — a coin toss at the start decides which colour you play.
The board uses a subtle checkerboard pattern in two shades of green, just like in the real game.
The four central squares form the starting formation — control around this area early.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On your turn, click or tap any square that shows a white dot — those are your legal placement squares. Once you click a valid square, your disc is placed there and all sandwiched opponent discs flip immediately. You have 20 seconds per move; if time expires, a random legal move is made for you automatically.
step1.clickSquare: Click a highlighted square to place your disc
step1.tapSquare: Tap a highlighted square to place your disc
step1.timer: 20 s per move — random move on timeout
tips: Translucent white dots mark all squares where you can legally place a disc this turn.
You cannot skip a turn voluntarily — you must play a legal move if one exists.
The timer resets to 20 s after every move, including the opponent's response.

step2.title: Placing Pieces & Flipping
step2.description: You may only place a disc on an empty square that outflanks at least one straight line of the opponent's discs — meaning your new disc and an existing disc of yours sandwich one or more enemy discs in a straight line (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal). All sandwiched discs immediately flip to your colour. A move that does not flip anything is illegal.
step2.rule: New disc + existing disc must sandwich ≥ 1 enemy disc in a straight line
tips: All flippable lines are processed at once — a single placement can flip in up to 8 directions.
A disc placed in a corner can never be flipped — it anchors an entire edge.
Diagonals count! Many beginners overlook diagonal sandwiching and miss strong moves.

step3.title: Valid Moves & Passing
step3.description: On each turn the board highlights every square where you can legally place a disc. If you have no valid moves, your turn is passed automatically and play moves to your opponent. If neither player has a valid move — which can happen before the board is full — the game ends immediately and the player with more discs wins.
step3.dotHint: Dots = all squares where you can legally place this turn
step3.passHint: No legal moves? Your turn is skipped automatically
tips: Having fewer legal moves is often strategically better — it means the opponent has less control.
The game can end before the board is full if both players are simultaneously locked out.
Watch the dot count each turn: a sudden drop in your options is a warning sign.

step4.title: Corners & Key Squares
step4.description: The four corner squares (highlighted in yellow) are the most valuable positions on the board — a disc placed there can never be flipped. This makes corners permanent anchors for entire edges. Conversely, the squares immediately adjacent to corners (the X- and C-squares) are dangerous: if you occupy them and the opponent takes the corner, they flip back and the corner is lost.
step4.cornerHint: Corners anchor entire edges — never lose them to the opponent
tips: Avoid the X-squares (diagonally adjacent to corners) unless you are certain the opponent cannot immediately take the corner.
C-squares (edge squares next to corners) are also risky — they give the opponent a path to the corner.
Controlling edge squares is generally safer than interior squares because they limit flip directions.

step5.title: End Game & Scoring
step5.description: The game ends when the board is full, or when neither player can make a legal move. Every disc on the board is counted — the player with the most discs wins. There are no points for move quality; only the final disc count matters. A draw occurs if both players finish with exactly 32 discs each.
tips: A late-game swing can flip dozens of discs in one move — never give up if the board is not full.
Forcing the opponent into bad positions (near corners) often matters more than raw disc count mid-game.
The final 10–15 moves are often the most decisive — preserve good positional options for the endgame.

step6.title: Game Modes & Difficulty
step6.description: CPU mode offers three difficulty levels. Easy plays random legal moves and will often walk into corners. Medium uses minimax search at depth 2, weighing positional values. Hard uses minimax at depth 4 with the full position weight matrix — it prioritises corners, edges, and mobility aggressively. Online mode matches you against real players via ELO-based matchmaking with a shared 20-second move timer. A coin toss assigns Black or White at the start of every game.
step6.coinToss: Coin toss assigns Black / White each game
tips: Easy CPU often plays into corners on accident — take advantage of every corner it offers.
Hard CPU uses positional weights: corners = 120 pts, X-squares = -40 pts, edges = ~20 pts.
CPU games do not affect your ELO — only Online matches count toward your rating.

step7.title: Online Play & ELO
step7.description: Online mode connects you to real opponents near your ELO rating. Before the game starts you will see your opponent's ELO and your estimated win chance — a higher percentage means the system expects you to win based on rating difference. After each online game your ELO updates: wins gain points, losses subtract, and draws are roughly neutral. You can forfeit an ongoing game at any time.
tips: Win chance above 60% means you are the favourite — below 40% you are the underdog.
Beating a higher-rated opponent earns significantly more ELO than beating an equal one.
Forfeiting counts as a loss — only resign when the board position is truly unrecoverable.

step0.title: Welcome to Backgammon
step0.description: Backgammon is a two-player race game played on a board of 24 narrow triangles called points. Each player has 15 checkers and moves them in opposite directions around the board — White moves from point 24 toward point 1, Black from point 1 toward point 24. The first player to bear off (remove) all 15 checkers wins. Dice determine how far you can move each turn.
tips: Points are numbered 1–24. White's home board is points 1–6 (bottom right), Black's is points 19–24 (top right).
White starts with: 2 on point 24, 5 on point 13, 3 on point 8, 5 on point 6.
A coin toss determines which colour you play — the board flips automatically so your checkers are always at the bottom.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: Each turn begins with you pressing the Roll Dice button. After rolling, purple-highlighted points show which of your checkers can move this turn. Click or tap a highlighted checker to select it — the valid destination points will light up with pink circles. Then click or tap a pink circle to complete the move. You have 20 seconds per turn; if time expires, a random legal move is made automatically.
step1.clickChecker: Click a highlighted checker to select
step1.clickDest: Click a pink circle to move there
step1.tapChecker: Tap a highlighted checker to select
step1.tapDest: Tap a pink circle to move there
step1.timer: 20 s per turn — auto-move on timeout
tips: Purple highlighting on a point means you have at least one checker there that can legally move.
If you re-click a selected checker, the selection clears — click another movable checker to switch.
The timer also runs during the CPU's turn so both players see real-time pressure.

step2.title: Dice & Movement
step2.description: Each turn you roll two dice. You must use both dice values as separate moves — for example, rolling 3 and 5 means you move one checker 3 points and another (or the same) checker 5 points. White moves toward lower-numbered points; Black moves toward higher-numbered points. If only one die can be used, you must play the higher value if possible.
tips: You cannot move to a point occupied by 2 or more opponent checkers — it is blocked.
If neither die value is playable, your turn is forfeited — this is rare but legal.
Using both dice is mandatory; you cannot choose to use only one when both are playable.

step3.title: Hitting & the Bar
step3.description: A point with only one checker of either colour is called a blot — it is vulnerable to attack. If you land on a blot, that opponent checker is hit and sent to the bar (the centre strip). A player with one or more checkers on the bar must re-enter them into the opponent's home board before moving any other checker. Re-entry uses the dice: a roll of N enters from the bar onto point N for Black, or 25-N for White.
step3.hit: Hit! Opponent checker goes to BAR
step3.reenter: Must re-enter from bar before moving anything else
tips: A point with 2+ checkers of the same colour is a prime — impossible to land on and safe from hits.
If your re-entry point is blocked by the opponent, you lose that turn (or part of it).
Hitting is powerful but leaves your own checker exposed if you land on a single checker too.

step4.title: Doubles
step4.description: When both dice show the same value — known as doubles — you get to use that value four times instead of the usual two. Rolling double 4s, for example, gives you four moves of 4 points each, which you must use to move one or more checkers. Unused moves of a doubles roll are simply forfeited at the end of the turn.
step4.fourMoves: Rolling doubles grants 4 moves of the same value — a huge tempo advantage
tips: Doubles rolls are the single biggest tempo swing in backgammon — they can advance your home board by 4 points in one turn.
You must use as many of the 4 sub-moves as possible; unused moves are lost only if no legal play exists.
Rolling double 6s (the highest doubles) is called a 'boxcar' and is the strongest possible roll.

step5.title: Bearing Off
step5.description: Once all 15 of your checkers are in your home board (points 1–6 for White, 19–24 for Black) you may start bearing off — removing checkers from the board entirely. Use dice values to remove checkers from the corresponding points, or move them closer if the exact point is empty. The first player to bear off all 15 checkers wins. If you still have checkers on the bar or outside your home board, bearing off is not yet allowed.
step5.offZone: Pink 'OFF' zone — bear a checker off here
step5.condition: All 15 checkers must be in home board first
tips: If you roll a number higher than any occupied point, you must bear off from the highest occupied point.
Winning by bearing off while the opponent still has checkers in your home board is a gammon — in online play, this awards bonus ELO.
Keep your home board as compact as possible before bearing off so there are fewer gaps to fill.

step6.title: Game Modes & Difficulty
step6.description: CPU mode offers three difficulty levels. Easy plays random legal moves and is good for learning the rules. Medium uses minimax search at depth 2 and makes reasonable positional choices. Hard uses depth 4 with advanced positional evaluation — it blocks aggressively, hits blots, and creates strong primes. Online mode matches you against real players via ELO-based matchmaking with a shared 20-second move timer. A coin toss assigns White or Black each game.
step6.coinToss: Coin toss assigns White / Black each game
tips: Easy CPU will frequently leave blots in dangerous positions — hit them aggressively.
Hard CPU prioritises blocking (making primes of 3+ consecutive points) and hitting your lone checkers.
CPU games do not affect your ELO — only Online matches update your rating.

step7.title: Online Play & ELO
step7.description: Online mode connects you to real opponents near your ELO rating. Before the game starts you will see your opponent's ELO and your estimated win chance — a higher percentage means you are the rating favourite. After each online game your ELO updates: wins gain points, losses subtract, and draws are roughly neutral. A gammon (bearing off while opponent is still in your home board) awards additional ELO. You can forfeit an ongoing game at any time.
tips: Win chance above 60% means you are the favourite — below 40% you are the underdog.
Beating a higher-rated opponent earns significantly more ELO than beating an equal one.
Forfeiting counts as a loss and deducts ELO — only resign when recovery is impossible.

step0.title: Welcome to Blackjack
step0.description: Blackjack is a card game where you compete against the dealer — not other players. Your goal is to build a hand with a total as close to 21 as possible without going over. If your total exceeds 21, you bust and lose immediately. The dealer plays by fixed rules: they must draw cards until they reach 17 or more, then stop. No real money is involved — all chips are virtual and for fun only.
tips: You always play against the dealer — other players have no effect on your hand.
The canvas shows dealer cards at the top and your hand at the bottom — just like a real table.
Number cards show their face value; Jacks, Queens, and Kings are each worth 10.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, click any button below the canvas to act. On mobile, tap the same buttons. During the betting phase, use the − and + buttons or the preset shortcuts (Min, 25%, 50%, Max) to set your wager. Once you press Deal, the cards are dealt and you must act on your hand. All buttons are clearly labeled and appear only when the action is available.
tips: Action buttons appear and disappear based on the current phase — you will never see an action that is not available.
The bet preset buttons use a percentage of your current maximum bet (25% of your chips), not a fixed amount.
Pressing Menu at any time returns you to the main screen without affecting your chip count.

step2.title: Card Values
step2.description: Each card has a point value. Number cards (2–9) are worth their face value. Face cards — Jack, Queen, and King — are each worth 10. The Ace is special: it counts as either 1 or 11, whichever keeps your hand at 21 or below. A hand using an Ace as 11 is called a soft hand; if drawing another card would bust you, the Ace automatically drops to 1.
tips: Aces are extremely powerful — they give your hand flexibility and are the key to soft hands.
A soft hand (Ace counted as 11) cannot bust on the next draw — the Ace simply reverts to 1.
Two decks are shuffled together at the start of each game, giving a total of 104 cards.

step3.title: Hit & Stand
step3.description: Hit draws one more card from the deck and adds it to your hand. You can hit as many times as you like as long as your total stays at 21 or below. Stand ends your turn and passes control to the dealer. Once you stand, the dealer reveals their hidden card and draws until reaching 17 or more. If your total is higher than the dealer's (or the dealer busts), you win even money — you get back your bet plus the same amount.
tips: Basic strategy: stand on 17 or above, hit on 8 or below, and use judgment for 9–16.
If the dealer shows a 7 or higher, hit aggressively — the dealer is likely to make 17–21.
Busting is immediate — you lose even if the dealer would also have busted on their next draw.

step4.title: Double Down & Split
step4.description: Double Down is available on your first two cards only: you double your bet and receive exactly one more card, then stand automatically. This is powerful when you have 9, 10, or 11 and the dealer shows a weak card. Split is available when both starting cards have the same rank: you pay another bet equal to your original, and each card becomes the start of a separate hand — each played out individually.
step4.doubleHint: Double bet → draw exactly 1 card → auto-stand
step4.splitHint: Same rank → 2 separate hands, each with its own bet
tips: Always split Aces and 8s — splitting Aces gives two strong starting hands, splitting 8s escapes a weak 16.
Double down when your two-card total is 10 or 11 and the dealer shows 2–9 — this is among the strongest plays.
Never split 10-value cards (10, J, Q, K) — a hard 20 is almost always the best hand you can have.

step5.title: Blackjack & Dealer Rules
step5.description: A natural Blackjack is an Ace plus any 10-value card as your first two cards — it pays 1.5× your bet (e.g., bet 2.00 → win 3.00 returned plus 2.00 bet = 5.00 total). If both you and the dealer have Blackjack it is a push. If your final total ties the dealer's, it is also a push — you get your bet back exactly. The dealer must stand on any total of 17 or more (including soft 17), so the dealer can never keep drawing once they hit 17.
step5.dealerHint: Dealer must draw until ≥ 17, then stop
tips: A push returns your bet — it is neither a win nor a loss, so your chip total stays the same.
Blackjack beats a dealer total of 21 made with three or more cards — the 1.5× bonus only applies to two-card 21.
If you bust before the dealer draws, you lose immediately — the dealer does not even need to play.

step6.title: Chips & No Real Money
step6.description: This is a completely free, no-stakes game — there is no real money involved at any point. You start with virtual chips and your balance is saved between sessions. If your chip count ever falls below 10, it is automatically topped up back to 10 so you can always keep playing. The maximum bet per round is 25% of your current chip total, which keeps the game balanced and prevents you from losing everything in one hand.
step6.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · chips are virtual · for fun only
step6.floorHint: Chips always topped up to 10 minimum — you never run out
step6.maxBetHint: Max bet per round = 25% of current chips
tips: Your chip count is saved automatically after every round — you can close the game and resume anytime.
The 25% bet cap means you need at least 1.00 chip to place the minimum bet of 0.25.
Even if you lose many rounds in a row, the 10-chip floor guarantees you can always play at least one more hand.

step7.title: High Score
step7.description: Your high score is the highest chip count you have ever reached in a session. It is displayed in the header alongside your current chip balance. Build your chip stack by winning rounds, landing Blackjacks, and using Double Down wisely. Blackjacks pay 1.5× and are the single biggest boost to your balance — catching them consistently is the key to a high score.
step7.winHint: Winning a regular round pays 1:1 — bet 2.00, win 2.00
step7.blackjackHint: Blackjack pays 1.5× — the fastest way to grow your chip stack
step7.highScoreHint: High score updates automatically when you beat your personal best
tips: Consistent play beats gambling big — small steady wins accumulate faster than occasional double-downs.
Splitting Aces effectively doubles your chance of landing a Blackjack in the same round.
Your high score is stored on the server and persists across devices.

step0.title: Welcome to Baccarat
step0.description: Baccarat is a card-comparison game where you bet on which side — Player or Banker — will have a hand closer to 9, or whether the round will end in a Tie. You make no decisions once the cards are dealt: the drawing rules are completely automatic. Your only choice is where to place your bet before each round begins. No real money is involved — all chips are virtual and purely for fun.
tips: Baccarat is one of the simplest casino games — there are no strategy decisions after you place your bet.
The canvas shows Banker cards at the top and Player cards at the bottom, just like a real Baccarat table.
A natural (8 or 9 on the first two cards) ends the round immediately with no further draws.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: Before dealing, select your bet type by clicking or tapping one of the three option buttons — Player, Tie, or Banker. Then set your bet amount using the − and + buttons or the preset shortcuts (Min, 25%, 50%, Max). Press Deal to start the round. Cards are dealt and resolved automatically — you watch the outcome and then proceed to the next round. There are no in-round decisions.
step1.clickBet: Click a bet type to select it
step1.clickDeal: Click Deal to start the round
step1.tapBet: Tap a bet type to select it
tips: Your selected bet type stays active between rounds — you do not need to re-select it every time.
The bet amount preset shortcuts are based on your current maximum bet (25% of chips), not a fixed value.
Pressing Menu returns to the main screen at any time without changing your chip count.

step2.title: Card Values
step2.description: Baccarat uses a unique scoring system. Aces are worth 1. Cards 2–9 are worth their face value. Tens, Jacks, Queens, and Kings are all worth 0. Hands are totalled and then reduced modulo 10 — meaning only the last digit counts. For example, 7 + 8 = 15, which becomes 5. This means the highest possible hand value is 9, and you can never bust in Baccarat.
step2.modRule: Only the last digit counts — you can never bust
tips: A hand of 9 is the best possible — often called a 'natural nine' if achieved on the first two cards.
Because 10/J/Q/K = 0, drawing one of them to a strong hand (like 7) keeps your total unchanged.
The mod-10 rule means a two-card hand of K + 9 = 9, which is a natural — despite the King.

step3.title: Bet Options
step3.description: There are three bets available each round. Player pays 1:1 — bet 2.00, win 2.00. Banker pays 0.95:1 — a 5% commission is taken because the Banker side wins slightly more often; bet 2.00, win 1.90. Tie pays 8:1 — both sides score the same total; bet 2.00, win 16.00. If you bet Player or Banker and the round ends in a Tie, you receive your bet back as a push.
step3.tieHint: Win pays 8:1 · push on Banker/Player bets
tips: Banker is statistically the best bet with the lowest house edge — the 5% commission accounts for this advantage.
The Tie bet has an 8:1 payout but a high house edge — it is exciting but not recommended as a primary strategy.
If you bet Player and the round ends in a Tie, you get your bet back; you do not lose it.

step4.title: Drawing Rules
step4.description: All drawing is automatic — you never choose whether to draw. A natural (either side scores 8 or 9 on the first two cards) ends the round immediately. Otherwise, Player draws a third card if their total is 0–5 and stands on 6–7. Banker's drawing rule is more complex: it depends on the Banker's current total and, if the Player drew a third card, what value that card was. The full Banker table is applied automatically every time.
step4.naturalHint: Natural 8 or 9 → no draws, round ends immediately
step4.bankerComplex: Complex table based on Player's 3rd card
tips: You never need to know the Banker drawing table — the game applies it automatically every round.
Player drawing on 0–5 means the Player side draws a third card more often than not.
Understanding naturals is the only rule you really need: if either side gets 8 or 9 on two cards, the round ends.

step5.title: Round Result
step5.description: After all draws are resolved, the side with the higher total wins. The result overlay shows the winning side and your outcome. If you correctly predicted the winner, your bet is returned plus your winnings based on the payout rate you selected. If you bet on the losing side, your bet is lost. The round is then complete and you can adjust your bet and start the next one.
tips: Winning on Banker with a 2.00 bet returns 2.00 + 1.90 = 3.90 total (5% commission deducted).
Winning on a Tie with a 1.00 bet returns 1.00 + 8.00 = 9.00 total — the highest payout in the game.
After each result, your chips are updated instantly and the next round can begin immediately.

step6.title: Chips & No Real Money
step6.description: This is a completely free, no-stakes game — no real money is involved at any point. You start with virtual chips and your balance is saved between sessions. If your chip count ever falls below 10, it is automatically restored to 10 so you can always keep playing. The maximum bet per round is capped at 25% of your current chips, which keeps the game balanced across sessions.
step6.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · chips are virtual · for fun only
step6.floorHint: Chips always restored to 10 minimum — you never run out
step6.maxBetHint: Max bet per round = 25% of current chips
tips: Your chip count is saved automatically after every round — you can close the game and resume at any time.
The 25% bet cap means you need at least 1.00 chip to place the minimum bet of 0.25.
Even after a long losing streak, the 10-chip floor guarantees you can always place one more bet.

step7.title: High Score
step7.description: Your high score is the highest chip count you have ever reached in this game. It is displayed in the header next to your current balance. Grow your chip stack by placing consistent bets and landing a Tie payout — the 8:1 Tie win is the single biggest chip multiplier available. Your high score is stored automatically and persists across sessions.
step7.winHint: Winning Player pays 1:1 — steady and safe
step7.tieHint: Winning Tie pays 8:1 — the biggest single-round boost
step7.highScoreHint: High score updates automatically when you beat your personal best
tips: Consistently betting Banker is statistically the most chip-efficient strategy over many rounds.
Occasional Tie bets are high risk but the 8:1 payout can push your score far above your current level.
Your high score is stored on the server and is visible across all your devices.

step0.title: Welcome to Poker
step0.description: This is Texas Hold'em — the most popular form of poker. You sit at a table with 3 AI opponents, each given a chip stack 3 to 4 times your own. Every player is dealt 2 private hole cards, and 5 community cards are revealed over four betting rounds. Your goal is to make the best 5-card hand using any combination of your 2 hole cards and the 5 community cards — or to bluff every opponent into folding before the showdown. No real money is involved; all chips are virtual.
tips: Your 2 hole cards are face-up only to you — opponents see them as face-down dark-green cards.
Community cards appear in the centre of the table and are shared by all players still in the hand.
You win the pot by having the best hand at showdown — or by being the last player who has not folded.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, click any action button below the canvas when it is your turn. On mobile, tap the same buttons. Action buttons appear and disappear automatically based on the current game state — you will only ever see actions that are valid. When you can raise, a raise slider appears: use the − / + buttons or the preset shortcuts (Min, ½ Pot, Pot, Max) to choose your raise size, then press Raise to confirm.
step1.raiseHint: Raise slider appears only when you can raise
tips: The Fold button is always available on your turn — you can fold at any point, even if checking is free.
Check is only available when no one has raised in the current betting round — it passes without paying.
The raise slider presets use pot-relative sizing: Min is the minimum legal raise, Pot raises to the full pot size.

step2.title: Blinds & Betting Streets
step2.description: Before cards are dealt, the two players left of the dealer post forced bets called blinds — the Small Blind (1 chip) and the Big Blind (2 chips). These seed the pot and ensure there is always something to play for. Play then proceeds through four streets: Preflop (hole cards only), Flop (first 3 community cards revealed), Turn (4th community card), and River (5th and final card). Each street has a round of betting before the next cards are dealt.
tips: The dealer position rotates clockwise every round, so the blind obligations shift — no one pays permanently.
A 1% join fee is deducted from your chip stack each time you start a new round, before blinds are posted.
If everyone folds to a blind, the blind wins the pot without a showdown — protecting your blind is valid strategy.

step3.title: Hand Rankings
step3.description: Hands are ranked from strongest to weakest. The best possible hand is a Royal Flush (A K Q J 10 all in the same suit), which beats everything. Below that, each category beats all lower ones. When two players hold the same category, the winner is determined by the highest cards in that category — for example, a pair of Aces beats a pair of Kings. If hands are completely tied, the pot is split evenly between all tied players.
tips: You only need to remember the top 5 — Royal Flush, Straight Flush, Four of a Kind, Full House, Flush. Everything below is intuitive.
Straights and Flushes are easier to make than players expect — if the board has 3 suited cards, someone may have a flush.
Ace plays both high (A-K-Q-J-10) and low (5-4-3-2-A) in straights — it is the only card that works both ways.

step4.title: Betting Actions
step4.description: On your turn you choose one of up to five actions. Fold gives up your hand and any chips already bet. Check passes your turn at no cost (only when no one has raised). Call matches the current highest bet. Raise increases the bet — every other player must then call your raise, re-raise, or fold. All-In bets every chip you have left; even if opponents bet more, you can only win up to the amount you put in from each player.
step4.hint: Three 7s — a set — is a strong hand
tips: Three of a Kind (a 'set' or 'trips') is strong enough to raise or even go all-in on most boards.
Raising after a flop that helps your hand charges opponents to draw cards that can beat you — do not just call.
Going all-in with a weak hand as a bluff can work, but the AI opponents call all-ins fairly often — choose your spots.

step5.title: Showdown
step5.description: After the final betting round on the River, if two or more players remain, there is a showdown: all remaining hands are revealed face-up and the best 5-card hand wins the entire pot. The game automatically evaluates all hands, highlights the winner's cards in gold, and displays the result. If your hand ties with an opponent's, the pot is split evenly. After the showdown you can continue to the next round or return to the main menu.
tips: The game evaluates the best 5-card combination from your 2 hole cards and all 5 community cards automatically.
Even if you feel certain you are behind, you can call a small bet on the river if the pot odds justify it.
After a showdown you can see the AI's cards — use this to understand how they play and adjust.

step6.title: Chips & No Real Money
step6.description: This game uses virtual chips only — no real money is ever involved. You start with 10 chips and your balance is saved between sessions. If your chip count drops to zero you are considered broke and can restart with the 10-chip floor guarantee. A 1% join fee is deducted at the start of each new round to simulate a small rake; this keeps the game balanced across many sessions. The AI opponents receive chip stacks 3 to 4 times your stack each round.
step6.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · chips are virtual · for fun only
step6.floorHint: Chips always restored to 10 minimum when you are broke — you can always restart
step6.joinFeeHint: 1% of your chips is deducted as a join fee at the start of every new round
tips: Your chip count is saved after every round — close the game and resume exactly where you left off.
The AI starts each round with 3–4× your chips, so you are always the underdog in raw stack size — use strategy.
Even at 10 chips (the floor), you can post the blinds and play at least one full round.

step7.title: High Score
step7.description: Your high score is the highest chip count you have ever reached. It is displayed in the header alongside your current balance. Grow your stack by winning pots, making well-timed all-ins, and correctly reading when to fold. The fastest way to accumulate chips is to be aggressive with strong hands while minimising losses when you are likely behind — consistent disciplined play beats occasional lucky all-ins over the long run.
step7.winHint: Each pot won adds directly to your chip stack — no payout multipliers
step7.handHint: Strong hands like Full House and Four of a Kind win big pots that jump your high score quickly
step7.highScoreHint: High score updates automatically when you beat your personal best and is stored on the server
tips: Folding often is not weakness — preserving chips for strong spots is the foundation of winning poker.
The AI raises and calls fairly aggressively, so do not bluff into multiple opponents; pick spots against single players.
Your high score is global across devices — improving it reflects genuine skill growth over many sessions.

step0.title: Welcome to Canasta
step0.description: Canasta is a 4-player card-melding game played across multiple rounds. You compete against 3 AI opponents on the same table, each trying to build melds — sets of 3 or more cards of the same rank — and eventually complete a Canasta (a meld of 7 or more cards). The first player to reach 3000 cumulative points wins the game. Rounds continue until someone crosses that threshold. No real money is involved; all chips are virtual.
tips: A Canasta of 7 cards without any wild cards is a Natural Canasta (+500 pts) — the highest-value single meld.
You must complete at least one Canasta before you are allowed to go out and end the round.
The scoreboard strip at the bottom of the canvas shows every player's running total towards 3000.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, click cards in your hand to select them (selected cards lift up), then click action buttons. On mobile, tap cards to select and tap actions to execute. Each turn has two phases: first Draw (draw from the deck or take the discard pile), then Meld (meld cards, add to existing melds, and finally discard one card to end your turn). All six action buttons appear only when the relevant action is valid.
step1.turnHint: Draw → Meld / Add / Discard → End turn
tips: You must discard exactly one card to end your turn — clicking Discard locks in your selected card.
You can meld multiple groups in a single turn before discarding — there is no limit to how much you meld.
Go Out pulses in purple and only appears when you have a Canasta and exactly one card left to discard.

step2.title: Card Types
step2.description: The 108-card deck (two standard decks plus 4 Jokers) contains four distinct card types. Natural cards (4s through Ks and Aces) are used to form melds. Wild cards (Jokers worth 50 pts, and 2s worth 20 pts) substitute for any natural card in a meld but cannot outnumber the natural cards in that meld. Red Threes (3♥ 3♦) are automatically removed from your hand and placed aside — they score +100 pts each only if you have at least one meld; otherwise they score −100 each. Black Threes (3♣ 3♠) score 5 pts but can only be discarded — you cannot meld them.
step2.wildHint: Joker (50 pts) and 2 (20 pts) — substitute any rank
step2.redThreeHint: Auto-collected · ±100 pts depending on whether you have melds
step2.blackThreeHint: Discard only · freezes pile if discarded as a wild
tips: Wild cards are extremely valuable — a Joker or 2 can turn a weak natural pair into a valid meld of 3.
Red Threes are collected automatically when you draw them — no action needed, they go straight to your red-three zone.
Do not discard wild cards unless you have to — they are among the highest-scoring cards in the game.

step3.title: Melding
step3.description: Select 3 or more cards of the same rank and press Meld to lay them on the table as a new meld. At least 2 of the selected cards must be natural (non-wild). Wild cards can fill the rest, but wilds can never equal or outnumber the naturals in a meld. If this is your first meld of the game, the cards you meld must total at least 50 points (or 90/120 as your cumulative score grows). After melding, you can add more cards to any of your existing melds using Add to Meld.
step3.maxWilds: Wilds must be fewer than naturals
tips: The minimum initial meld requirement increases as your cumulative score grows — plan for 90+ pts in later rounds.
Melds can be extended indefinitely — keep adding naturals and wilds until you reach 7 cards for a Canasta.
You can only add to your own melds — you cannot extend an AI player's meld.

step4.title: Canastas & Going Out
step4.description: A Canasta is any meld that reaches 7 or more cards. A Natural Canasta (no wild cards, 7+ cards) earns a +500 bonus on top of the card values. A Mixed Canasta (contains at least one wild, 7+ cards) earns +300. You must have completed at least one Canasta (natural or mixed) before you are allowed to go out. Going out means discarding your last card with no cards remaining in hand, earning a +100 bonus. Going out also ends the round for everyone.
tips: Aim for Natural Canastas whenever possible — the 200-point difference over Mixed compounds across rounds.
Going out earns +100 but also stops your opponents from extending their melds, so time it when you are ahead.
You can have multiple Canastas — each completed 7-card meld scores its bonus separately.

step5.title: Discard Pile & Freezing
step5.description: You can take the entire discard pile instead of drawing from the deck — but only if the top card is not a Black Three, not a wild, and you hold at least 2 natural cards matching the top card's rank. Taking the pile can give you a huge hand advantage. The pile is frozen when a wild card sits on top — a frozen pile requires you to hold 2 naturals matching the top card before you can take it. The pile also freezes permanently if a wild is discarded to it.
step5.frozenHint: Still need ≥2 naturals to take; wild card on top triggered this
tips: A large discard pile can be better than a full deck draw — timing a pile take can jump-start your melds.
Never discard a wild card carelessly — it freezes the pile and prevents you from easily taking it later.
If the pile is frozen and you need it, make sure you genuinely have 2 naturals matching the top card.

step6.title: Scoring & Chips
step6.description: This is a completely free game — no real money involved. Chips are virtual, saved between sessions, and always topped up to a minimum of 10 so you never run out. A chip bet is placed only once per full game (at the start of round 1) and is lost or won based on whether you win the game. In-round scoring is cumulative: Canasta bonuses, card values, red-three bonuses, and the go-out bonus all count. Cards left in hand at round end subtract from your score.
step6.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · chips are virtual · for fun only
tips: Cards in hand at round end subtract their point values from your score — try not to hold high-value cards late.
Four Red Threes held simultaneously are worth 800 points instead of 4×100 — an enormous bonus if you have melds.
Your chip balance is saved automatically. The minimum floor of 10 chips ensures you can always start a new game.

step7.title: Score Target & High Score
step7.description: The game ends when any player's cumulative score reaches or exceeds 3000 points — that player wins the chip pot. Rounds continue until that threshold is crossed, so a game can last many rounds. Your high score is the highest chip count you have ever held. Winning a full game awards you the combined bet pot from all players. Consistent Canasta-building, timely pile takes, and going out at the right moment are the keys to reaching 3000 first.
tips: Focus on completing Canastas early — a Natural Canasta in round 1 can create a commanding score lead.
Keep an eye on the scoreboard strip to see how close opponents are to 3000 — adjust aggression accordingly.
Your high score is stored on the server and reflects your chip wealth across all completed games.

step0.title: Welcome to Cee-Lo
step0.description: Cee-Lo is a dice game for 4 players — you and 3 AI opponents named Kauã, Angelo, and Miguel. Every round, all players bet their virtual tags into a shared pot, then take turns rolling 3 dice in the bowl. The player with the highest-ranked hand wins the entire pot. No real money is involved; all tags are virtual.
tips: Your 3 opponents each start every round with a tag stack close to yours — nobody has a huge chip advantage.
The bowl in the centre of the screen is where the dice are shaken; watch each player's card to see their result.
You win the whole pot — including all AI bets — if you roll the best hand. A big pot can double your stack.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, click the action buttons below the canvas on your turn. On mobile, tap the same buttons. The Roll button starts the round once you've set your bet. After all players have rolled and a winner is decided, use Next Round to play again or Menu to return to the main screen. Use the bet adjuster to set how many tags you wager — pick a preset (1, 10, 50, 100) or use − / + to fine-tune.
step1.betSliderHint: Bet adjuster — presets and manual fine-tune with − / +
tips: The Roll button is only active once you have placed a valid bet — make sure your bet is at least 1 tag.
You can only bet up to your available tags minus the 100-tag floor, so you can never go broke.
After a round ends the Next Round button resets the table; you can also leave any time via Menu.

step2.title: The Bowl & Rolling
step2.description: Each round, every player rolls 3 dice in the wooden bowl. If the result has no valid combination — no matching pair, no triple, and not 1-2-3 or 4-5-6 — the dice are re-rolled automatically until a valid hand comes up. You'll see the dice shake in the bowl and each player's result card update in real time as rolls are resolved one by one.
tips: No Combo (three completely different non-matching dice with no pair) is simply re-rolled — it never counts as a loss.
1-2-3 is the only instant-loss combo; rolling it means you automatically lose regardless of other players' hands.
4-5-6 is an instant win — if you roll it, you win the pot without any further comparison.

step3.title: Hand Rankings
step3.description: Hands are ranked from strongest to weakest. 4-5-6 is the highest (instant win). Trips (three of a kind) come next — higher number wins ties. Point hands (two matching dice set a point equal to the odd die) rank below trips — higher point wins. Finally, 1-2-3 is the instant-loss hand. If two players tie on the same rank, the pot is split between them.
step3.rerollNote: No Combo (no pair, not 4-5-6 or 1-2-3) → automatic re-roll
tips: Any trips hand beats any point hand — even Trips 1 (three 1s) beats Point 6.
Point is determined by the non-matching die when two dice are equal: 2-2-5 = Point 5.
If two players tie exactly — both roll Point 5, for example — the pot is split between them.

step4.title: Betting & The Pot
step4.description: Before rolling, you set your bet using the adjuster below the canvas. All 3 AI opponents then match your bet within 80–120% of your amount (capped by their available tags). The pot is the sum of all four bets. The winner collects the entire pot. You can bet as little as 1 tag or as much as your tags allow above the 100-tag floor.
step4.potNote: Pot = sum of all four bets — winner takes all
tips: AI bets 80–120% of your stake, so a larger bet from you creates a proportionally larger pot.
You cannot bet more than your total tags minus the 100-tag floor guarantee, so you can't lose everything.
Betting aggressively with a strong starting position can rapidly grow your tag count — but variance is high.

step5.title: Result
step5.description: After all four players have rolled, hands are compared. The player with the highest-ranked hand wins the pot — their card glows gold on the canvas. If two or more players tie, the pot is split evenly between them. If you win, your tags increase by the full pot amount. The result message shows your profit or loss, then you can play the next round.
step5.tieNote: Tie · Pot split between tied players
step5.loseNote: Lose · Tags deducted by your bet only
tips: On a tie the pot is split, so you get some chips back — it's not a full loss.
You only lose your own bet if an opponent wins, not the whole pot.
After the result, click Next Round immediately to keep playing — the bet resets to your last used amount.

step6.title: Virtual Tags & No Real Money
step6.description: This game uses virtual tags only — no real money is ever involved. You start with 100 tags and your balance is saved between sessions. If your tag count would ever drop below 100, it is automatically restored to 100 so you can always keep playing. The AI opponents each start every round with a stack similar to yours.
step6.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · tags are virtual · for fun only
step6.floorHint: Tags always restored to 100 minimum — you can never run out and can always play another round
step6.aiTagsHint: AI opponents start each round with ±10% of your current tag count
tips: Your tag count is saved after every round — close the game and resume exactly where you left off.
The 100-tag floor means there is no penalty for experimenting with large bets; you always have a safety net.
AI stacks are generated close to yours each round, keeping the game balanced no matter how much you've won.

step7.title: High Score
step7.description: Your high score is the highest tag count you have ever reached. It is displayed alongside your current balance at the top of the screen. Grow your stack by winning pots — especially when you can bet large with a strong hand. The fastest way to climb is to bet aggressively when variance is in your favour and cut losses quickly.
step7.winHint: Each pot won adds directly to your tag count — no multipliers
step7.bestHandHint: 4-5-6 or high Trips win massive pots that jump your high score fast
step7.highScoreHint: High score updates automatically when you beat your personal best and is stored on the server
tips: Your high score is persistent across devices — it reflects your all-time best session.
Big bets when you sense the dice are hot are the fastest route to a high score, but also the riskiest.
Consistent mid-size bets over many rounds can outperform a lucky all-in — steady play compounds.

step0.title: Welcome to Craps
step0.description: Craps is a solo dice game played against the house. Each round you pick a bet type, set your wager, and roll two dice. The first roll of a round is the come-out roll, which either resolves your bet immediately (a natural or craps) or sets a point number that you then try to hit before rolling a 7. No real money is involved — all chips are virtual.
tips: You play alone against the house — there are no other human or AI players at the table.
Every round starts fresh with a come-out roll. You choose your bet type before each roll.
The six betting zones at the bottom of the table show all available bets and their payouts at a glance.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, click any button below the canvas. On mobile, tap the same buttons. Press Play to start your first game, then Roll to throw the dice each turn. After a round resolves, Next Round returns you to the come-out phase, and Menu exits to the main screen. Use the amount adjuster (−/+) or presets (Min, 25%, 50%, Max) to set your wager, then pick your bet type from the coloured buttons.
step1.betTypeHint: Bet type buttons appear below the amount adjuster when you can change bets
tips: The Roll button stays disabled while the dice animation plays — wait for it to become active before rolling again.
You can change your bet type freely between rounds, but not mid-round during the point phase.
Bet type buttons are hidden during the point phase for Pass and Don't Pass — those bets lock in once the point is set.

step2.title: The Come-Out Roll
step2.description: The come-out roll is the first roll of every new round. The outcome depends entirely on the sum of the two dice. Roll a 7 or 11 (a natural) and most bets win immediately. Roll a 2, 3, or 12 (craps) and most bets lose immediately. Any other number — 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, or 10 — becomes the point, and the round continues into the point phase.
tips: 7 is the most likely single outcome when rolling two dice — it appears 6 out of 36 possible combinations.
Don't Pass wins on 2 or 3 but pushes on 12 on the come-out — the 12 rule is the house's edge on that bet.
If the come-out sets a point, the amber puck on the canvas will show the point number for the rest of the round.

step3.title: The Point Phase
step3.description: Once a point is established, you keep rolling until one of two things happens: you roll the point number (win for Pass bets) or you roll a 7, known as sevening-out (lose for Pass bets). Every other number is neutral — the dice are simply rolled again. The point puck on the canvas always shows which number you're chasing.
tips: The longer the point phase lasts, the more dramatic the tension — many rounds end quickly, but some can go on for many rolls.
7 is still the most common roll even in the point phase, which is why Pass bets are harder to win once a point is set.
Field and Any Seven bets are always resolved on every single roll — they are not affected by the point phase.

step4.title: Pass & Don't Pass
step4.description: Pass and Don't Pass are the two fundamental craps bets and the best starting point for new players. Pass bets with the shooter — you win on a natural (7 or 11) on the come-out and win if the point is made before a 7. Don't Pass bets against the shooter — you win on 2 or 3 on the come-out, push on 12, and win if a 7 appears before the point is made.
step4.passPoint: Point phase: roll point = win, 7 = lose
tips: Pass is the most beginner-friendly bet — rooting for 7 and 11 on the come-out is intuitive.
Don't Pass has a very slightly lower house edge than Pass because of the bar-12 push, making it marginally better value.
If you're unsure which to pick, start with Pass — it's the most common bet in real craps too.

step5.title: Field, Any Seven, Come & Don't Come
step5.description: Field is resolved on every roll: it wins on 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, or 11 (paying 1:1) with bonuses on 2 (2:1) and 12 (3:1), and loses on 5, 6, 7, or 8. Any Seven wins 4:1 if the next roll is a 7, and loses otherwise. Come and Don't Come work exactly like Pass and Don't Pass, but they are placed during the point phase, creating a secondary wager alongside your main bet.
step5.fieldDesc: Win on 2 (2:1), 3/4/9/10/11 (1:1), 12 (3:1). Lose on 5/6/7/8. Resolved every roll.
step5.anySevenDesc: Win 4:1 if next roll is 7. Lose on anything else. Resolved every roll.
step5.comeDesc: Like Pass but placed after the point is set. 7/11 = win, 2/3/12 = lose, other = come-point won.
step5.dontComeDesc: Like Don't Pass but placed after the point is set. 2/3 = win, 12 = push, 7/11 = lose.
tips: Field covers 7 out of 12 possible totals, but 5, 6, 7, and 8 — the most common rolls — all lose.
Any Seven is a high-variance bet: 4:1 pays well but you win less than 1 in 6 rolls on average.
Come and Don't Come are advanced bets — try Pass and Don't Pass first before experimenting with them.

step6.title: Virtual Chips & No Real Money
step6.description: This game uses virtual chips only — no real money is ever involved. You start with 10 chips and your balance is saved between sessions. If your chip count would drop below 10, it is automatically restored to 10 so you can always play another round. The maximum bet per roll is 25% of your current chips, preventing you from losing everything in a single roll.
step6.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · chips are virtual · for fun only
step6.floorHint: Chips always restored to 10 minimum — you can never run out and can always roll again
step6.maxBetHint: Max bet per roll is 25% of your chips — use the Max preset to find it quickly
tips: Your chip count is saved after every round — close the game and resume exactly where you left off.
The 10-chip floor means you always have enough to cover at least four minimum bets (0.25 chips each).
The 25% max-bet cap keeps each round meaningful without risking your entire stack on a single throw.

step7.title: High Score
step7.description: Your high score is the highest chip count you have ever reached. It is shown alongside your current balance at the top of the screen. Grow your stack by winning rounds with well-chosen bets and smart bet sizing. The fastest path to a high score is using higher-payout bets like Any Seven at the right moment — but consistent Pass bets with good sizing will win over the long run.
step7.winHint: Each winning roll adds directly to your chip stack — payouts vary by bet type
step7.bestBetHint: Any Seven pays 4:1 — landing a few of those in a row can spike your high score fast
step7.highScoreHint: High score updates automatically when you beat your personal best and is stored on the server
tips: Your high score is global across devices — improving it reflects genuine understanding of the game.
Stick to Pass or Don't Pass for stable growth; use Field or Any Seven sparingly for explosive rounds.
Maximise your bet size when you're on a winning streak — the 25% cap means wins compound quickly.

step0.title: Welcome to Sic Bo
step0.description: Sic Bo is a solo dice game played against the house. You roll 3 dice and bet on the outcome before each roll. There are five bet types — Small, Big, Total, Double, and Triple — each with its own payout. The higher the risk, the bigger the reward. No real money is involved; all chips are virtual.
tips: Sic Bo is a pure chance game — there is no strategy that changes the odds, but choosing higher-risk bets gives bigger swings.
The 5 bet zones are always visible at the bottom of the canvas so you can see your active bet at a glance.
You play alone against the house — no opponents, no bluffing, just you and the dice.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, click the buttons below the canvas. On mobile, tap the same buttons. Press Play to start, then Roll to throw the dice after placing your bet. After the result, Next Round resets the table and Menu returns to the main screen. Use the amount adjuster (−/+) or presets (Min, 25%, 50%, Max) to set your wager, then pick your bet type from the row of category buttons.
step1.betTypeHint: Active bet type is highlighted in the category row below the amount adjuster
tips: The Roll button stays disabled while the dice are animating — wait a moment before clicking again.
Total, Double, and Triple bets reveal a sub-value picker after you select them — choose your specific number there.
You can change your bet type and value freely between rounds; your amount is remembered automatically.

step2.title: Small & Big
step2.description: Small and Big are the most beginner-friendly bets. Small wins when the sum of the 3 dice is 4–10, and Big wins when the sum is 11–17. Both pay 1:1. However, any triple (three identical dice) voids both bets — you lose regardless of the sum. This is the house's edge on these otherwise even bets.
step2.tripleVoids: Any triple voids both Small and Big
tips: Small and Big each cover nearly half of all outcomes — they're the safest bets in the game.
The triple void is rare but is the only way to lose a Small or Big bet on an 'eligible' total.
Start with Big or Small while learning the game — once comfortable, experiment with Total for better payouts.

step3.title: Total Bet
step3.description: The Total bet lets you predict the exact sum of all 3 dice, from 4 to 17. Extreme totals (4 and 17) are very rare and pay 60:1. Middle totals (9–12) are the most common and pay 6:1. After selecting Total as your bet type, a sub-value picker appears — tap or click the number you want to bet on. The payout multiplier for each total is shown next to it.
step3.pickHint: Sub-value picker appears when Total is selected
tips: Totals 9, 10, 11, and 12 cover the most likely outcomes — landing them pays 6:1 and happens fairly often.
Totals 4, 16, and 17 pay 60:1 but each has only 3 or fewer combinations out of 216 — extremely rare.
Mixing a Small/Big bet with a Total bet on the same round isn't possible — you can only have one active bet.

step4.title: Double & Triple
step4.description: Double wins when at least two of the three dice show the same specific face you picked. It pays 10:1. Triple wins when all three dice show the same face. Any Triple (any face) pays 30:1, and a Specific Triple (you pick the exact number, e.g. three 6s) pays an enormous 180:1. Both Double and Triple use the sub-value picker to select which face you're targeting.
step4.doubleDesc: Two matching dice on your chosen face
step4.anyTripleDesc: All three dice show any identical face
step4.specificTripleDesc: All three dice show your chosen face exactly
tips: Double is a 10:1 bet that hits more often than it feels — with 3 dice there are multiple ways to land a pair.
Any Triple (30:1) wins whenever all three dice match regardless of the face, making it more likely than a Specific Triple.
Specific Triple at 180:1 is the highest payout in the game — only 6 out of 216 rolls produce one.

step5.title: Result
step5.description: After the dice settle, the game evaluates your bet instantly. If you win, the dice glow white and your chip delta is shown in green. If you lose, the result is shown in grey. The canvas displays the exact dice values and their sum, so you can see why you won or lost. Then use Next Round to play again with the same bet, or adjust your bet before rolling.
step5.bigLoseNote: Big would have lost — triple voids it
tips: The result overlay shows your dice total and exact roll, helping you track patterns over time.
Even a Double or Triple win doesn't protect against a bad run — every roll is fully independent.
After a loss, check if a different bet type would have won on that roll — it's useful to build intuition.

step6.title: Virtual Chips & No Real Money
step6.description: This game uses virtual chips only — no real money is ever involved. You start with 10 chips and your balance is saved between sessions. If your chip count drops to 10 or below, it is automatically restored to 10 so you can always keep playing. The maximum bet per roll is capped at 25% of your current chips.
step6.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · chips are virtual · for fun only
step6.floorHint: Chips always restored to 10 minimum — you can never run out and can always roll again
step6.maxBetHint: Max bet per roll is 25% of your chips — the Max preset finds this for you automatically
tips: Your chip count is saved after every round — close the game and resume exactly where you left off.
The 10-chip floor means you can always afford at least one minimum bet (0.25 chips) even at rock bottom.
The 25% max-bet cap keeps each roll meaningful without risking your entire stack at once.

step7.title: High Score
step7.description: Your high score is the highest chip count you have ever reached. It is displayed alongside your current balance at the top of the screen. Grow your stack by picking bets you understand and sizing your wagers smartly. Landing a high-payout bet like a Specific Triple when your chips are up is the fastest way to spike your all-time best.
step7.winHint: Each winning roll adds directly to your chip stack — payouts vary by bet type
step7.tripleHint: Specific Triple pays 180:1 — a single big hit can massively jump your high score
step7.highScoreHint: High score updates automatically when you beat your personal best and is stored on the server
tips: Your high score is persistent across devices — it reflects your all-time best chip count.
Stick to Small or Big for stable growth; save Triple bets for when you want a high-risk spike.
The 25% bet cap means doubling your chips takes at most 3 wins in a row at Max bet — very achievable.

step0.title: Welcome to Liar's Dice
step0.description: Liar's Dice is a bluffing game for 4 players — you and 3 AI opponents named Kauã, Angelo, and Miguel. Each player starts with 5 dice, rolled face-down so only you can see your own. Players take turns making increasingly bold claims about how many dice of a certain face exist across the entire table. Call someone's bluff to reveal the truth — the loser loses a die. Last player with dice wins.
tips: Your dice are visible only to you — the AI opponents see their own dice but never yours.
The green glow around a player's nameplate shows whose turn it is to bid.
You play for real stakes — set your initial bet before the game starts, and win 3× your bet if you outlast all opponents.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, click any button below the canvas. On mobile, tap the same buttons. Before a game starts, set your initial bet with the adjuster, then press Play. On your turn, use the QTY and FACE steppers to compose your bid, then press the Bid button to submit it. If a bid has been made, the Call Bluff button also appears — press it to challenge. After a reveal, Continue advances the game.
step1.bidHint: Quick presets +1 QTY and +1 FACE let you raise the current bid with one tap
tips: The Bid button shows your current bid as 'Bid 3×4' so you always see exactly what you're about to submit.
Call Bluff only appears when a bid has been made — you cannot challenge before the first bid of a round.
The +1 QTY and +1 FACE shortcuts raise the current bid by the minimum amount — useful for quick, safe raises.

step2.title: How Bidding Works
step2.description: On your turn you make a bid: a quantity and a face value, claiming there are at least that many dice showing that face across all players combined. Every new bid must be strictly higher than the last — you can raise the quantity, raise the face value (keeping the same quantity), or do both. The sequence of bids escalates until someone calls bluff.
step2.callBluffNote: Call Bluff to challenge — it ends the bidding
tips: A bid of '3×4' means you claim there are at least 3 fours somewhere among all dice at the table.
You can only raise — never lower — the current bid. If all valid raises seem too risky, call the bluff instead.
Early in a round, bids are safe to raise; as the round progresses, watch for bids that seem wildly high.

step3.title: Wild 1s
step3.description: Dice showing 1 are wild and count toward any face from 2 to 5. If someone bids '3×5', any 1s at the table also count as 5s for the purpose of resolving that bid. However, 1s are NOT wild for face 6 — a bid of '3×6' only counts actual 6s. This makes 6 bids riskier and harder to support, but also harder to call bluff on accurately.
step3.sixException: Face 6 is the only face where 1s are not wild
tips: With 20 dice at the start, roughly 3–4 of them will be 1s on average — these boost counts for faces 2–5 significantly.
When the current bid is on face 6, you cannot count your 1s — be more conservative about whether that bid can stand.
Bidding on face 6 can catch opponents off guard since they may not expect you to ignore your wildcards.

step4.title: Calling a Bluff
step4.description: If you think the current bid is impossible or unlikely, press Call Bluff. All dice are immediately revealed. The game counts how many dice actually show the claimed face (including wild 1s for faces 2–5). If the actual count meets or exceeds the bid, the challenger loses a die. If the count falls short, the bidder loses a die. Either way, all dice are re-rolled and a new round begins.
step4.loserOutcome: Bidder loses a die — bid was too high
tips: Call bluff when the bid exceeds the total dice on the table, or when you can count in your own dice that the claim is impossible.
Don't call too early — AI players tend to bid conservatively early in a round and bluff more as pressure builds.
After a reveal you can see all dice on the canvas — use that information in your next round's bidding.

step5.title: Losing Dice & Elimination
step5.description: The loser of each challenge loses exactly one die. A player eliminated from all 5 dice is out for the rest of the game. As players lose dice the total at the table shrinks, making high bids harder to justify. The last player with at least one die wins the game — and your payout if you are that last player standing.
step5.lastOneStanding: Last player with any dice wins
tips: Once a player is down to 1–2 dice they become less reliable as challengers — they often call bluff desperately.
When you have many dice, you can support higher bids; protect that advantage by not calling bluff recklessly.
Eliminating a strong AI player early shrinks the total dice pool and makes the game easier to read.

step6.title: Stakes & No Real Money
step6.description: Before each game you set an initial bet. If you win — being the last player standing — you earn 3× your bet. If you lose (any opponent outlasts you), you lose your bet. No real money is ever involved; all money is virtual. If your balance drops to $10 or below, it is automatically restored to $10 so you can always play another game.
step6.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · money is virtual · for fun only
step6.floorHint: Money always restored to $10 minimum — you can never run out and can always play again
tips: Your money is saved after every game — close the app and resume exactly where you left off.
The maximum initial bet is 75% of your current balance — this prevents a single loss from wiping you out completely.
The 3× win payout means one victory more than makes up for two losses — consistency matters more than luck.

step7.title: High Score
step7.description: Your high score is the highest money balance you have ever reached. It is shown alongside your current balance at the top of the screen. To grow it fast, combine a large initial bet with a strong bluffing game — a well-timed big-bet win can jump your high score dramatically. Consistent wins with moderate bets compound reliably over time.
step7.winHint: Each win earns 3× your initial bet — size your bet confidently when you feel in control
step7.bigBetHint: A single win at 75% max bet can nearly double your stack in one game
step7.highScoreHint: High score updates automatically when you beat your personal best and is stored on the server
tips: Your high score is global across devices — improving it reflects genuine skill at reading and bluffing.
AI opponents bid predictably once you learn their patterns — aggressive raises often signal they have a strong position.
The best time to call bluff is late in a round when the table has few dice left and the bid is climbing fast.

step0.title: Welcome to Roulette
step0.description: Roulette is a solo game played against the house. Each round you place one or more bets on a numbered mat, then the wheel spins and a ball lands on a number. There are 37 numbers — 0 through 36 — split between red, black, and green (zero). You win when the number satisfies your bet. No real money is involved; all chips are virtual.
tips: Roulette is a pure chance game — the house always has a small edge because 0 wins only on specific bets.
You can place multiple different bets in the same round, spreading your stake across the mat.
The last results are shown as colored bubbles at the top — handy for spotting streaks, though each spin is fully independent.

step1.title: Controls
step1.description: On PC, click any zone on the betting mat to place a chip there. On mobile, tap the same zones. After placing at least one bet, press Spin to start the wheel — or wait 15 seconds and it spins automatically. Clear Bets removes all chips from the mat. After the result, Next Round starts fresh betting. Menu returns to the main screen.
step1.clickBet: Click a mat zone to place a bet
step1.tapBet: Tap a mat zone to place a bet
step1.rightClickCycle: Right-click (PC) cycles through bet percentage presets without placing a chip
step1.timerHint: Auto-spins after 15 seconds if bets are placed
tips: Select your bet percentage first using the preset buttons (1% through 50%) — each click on the mat uses that fraction of your chips.
On PC, right-click anywhere on the mat to cycle the active bet percentage without placing a chip.
If the timer reaches zero while bets are placed, the wheel spins automatically — no need to press Spin.

step2.title: The Betting Mat
step2.description: The mat has three sections. The number grid in the middle shows all 37 numbers (0–36) laid out in 3 rows of 12 columns, coloured red or black. The 2:1 column labels on the right let you bet on an entire row. Below the grid are the Dozen strips (1–12, 13–24, 25–36) and the six even-money outside bets (Low, Even, Red, Black, Odd, High). Click or tap any zone to place a chip.
step2.clickCellHint: Click / tap any zone to place a chip there
tips: Hovering over any zone highlights it in gold — this helps you see exactly what numbers your bet covers before clicking.
The 0 cell is in the far-left corner of the number grid — betting straight on 0 pays 35:1 like any other number.
You can place chips on the same zone multiple times in one round to accumulate your stake there.

step3.title: Straight Bet (35:1)
step3.description: A Straight bet is placed on a single number — any number from 0 to 36. If the ball lands on exactly that number, you win 35 times your bet back (plus your original stake). It is the highest-payout bet in the game. To place it, click directly on the numbered cell on the mat.
step3.straightDesc: Wins only when the ball lands on that exact number — highest payout in the game
step3.zeroNote: Zero is a valid straight-bet target too — click the green 0 cell on the far left
tips: Straight bets have a 1-in-37 chance of winning (~2.7%) but pay 35:1, making them the most exciting high-risk option.
You can place straight bets on multiple different numbers in the same round to spread your chances.
Combining a straight bet on a number with an outside bet that also covers it doubles your return on that number.

step4.title: Outside Bets (1:1)
step4.description: The six even-money bets sit at the very bottom of the mat. Red and Black bet on the colour of the winning number. Even and Odd bet on whether it is divisible by 2. Low covers 1–18 and High covers 19–36. All six pay 1:1 — you get your bet back doubled. Importantly, zero (0) is neither red/black, even/odd, nor low/high — it loses all six outside bets.
step4.payoutNote: All six pay 1:1 — steady, lower-risk bets
step4.zeroVoids: Zero loses all six outside bets
tips: Outside bets cover roughly half the wheel each, making them the safest way to play if you prefer steady results.
Betting Red and Low together covers a different subset of numbers than either bet alone — a useful combination.
Since zero voids all outside bets, the house edge comes entirely from that one slot in 37.

step5.title: Dozens & Columns (2:1)
step5.description: The Dozen bets split 1–36 into three groups of twelve: 1–12, 13–24, and 25–36. Each pays 2:1. The Column bets work similarly but split by row on the mat instead of sequential ranges — each column label on the right edge of the grid covers its entire horizontal row of 12 numbers and also pays 2:1. Zero loses all dozen and column bets.
step5.columnNote: Zero loses all dozen and column bets — same as outside bets
tips: Dozens and columns each cover 12 numbers — they have a 12-in-37 hit rate (~32%) and pay 2:1, a solid middle ground.
The three columns follow the layout of the mat rows, not sequential numbers — row 3 contains 3, 6, 9, 12 … 36.
Combining a dozen with a column that partially overlaps gives you dense coverage of a specific range at lower cost.

step6.title: Placing Multiple Bets
step6.description: You are free to place chips on as many zones as you like in a single round. Your total stake is split across all chips on the mat. Each bet is evaluated independently when the ball lands — some may win while others lose. The header shows your total bet and remaining budget so you always know how much is at stake before pressing Spin.
step6.lastHint: Recent results shown as red / black / green bubbles in the header
tips: Placing an outside bet alongside a straight bet on a number it covers can boost your return significantly if that number hits.
Spreading chips too thin across the mat makes each individual bet very small — watch your remaining budget in the header.
Clear Bets resets everything at once, so use it quickly if you change your mind before the timer runs out.

step7.title: Virtual Chips & High Score
step7.description: This game uses virtual chips only — no real money is involved. You start with 10 chips and your balance is saved between sessions. If your chip count drops to 10, it is restored automatically so you can always keep playing. Your high score records your peak chip balance ever reached and is saved on the server.
step7.noRealMoneyHint: 100% free · chips are virtual · for fun only
step7.floorHint: Chips always restored to 10 minimum — you can never run out
step7.straightWinHint: A straight-bet win returns 36× your chip stake — a great way to spike your high score fast
step7.highScoreHint: High score updates automatically every round and is saved to the server
tips: Your chip count is saved after every result, so closing the game mid-session won't cause you to lose progress.
The 10-chip floor means you can always place at least one minimum bet — the game never ends.
Combining a straight bet at 5–10% of chips with safer outside bets is a popular way to chase a big win while staying in the game.

step0.title: Welcome to Slots
step0.description: Slots is a solo game against the house with 3 spinning reels and up to 5 paylines. Before each spin you choose which paylines to activate and how much to bet per line. When the reels stop, any active payline that shows a winning symbol combination pays out. All chips are virtual — no real money involved.
tips: The three reels stop one by one from left to right with a satisfying clunk sound — watch for matching symbols as each reel lands.
You can have multiple paylines winning in the same spin — winnings from all active lines are combined.
